title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit (Nitems = 150) to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. The preregistered plan specified paired baseline vs guarded conditions evaluated with a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps validator. The executed run used deterministic synthetic tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one shared model generation per item and model_calls_used = 150 rather than two model calls per pair. No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and therefore no guarded exclusions or replacements were performed. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile the preregistration→execution artifacts to explain why this run was uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection, document execution accounting and validator traces, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for audit designs that would be sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational adoption requires that measured benchmark performance reflects model capability rather than artifacts of dataset contamination or templated items leaked into model training data. Recent surveys and benchmark critiques highlight contamination and construct‑validity risks that can inflate apparent reliability.

Research question & contribution. We preregistered a confirmatory audit asking: under conservative deterministic detectors (exact normalized equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds, and provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? We contribute: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored confirmatory execution (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) with archived prompts, model outputs, and validator traces; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on 150 paired items; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why this particular run yielded a degenerate null outcome and prescribes concrete artifact‑grounded audit improvements.

Scope and framing. Crucially, the executed confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") produced by a deterministic task generator and employed shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). These execution facts, recorded in the archived model configuration and task manifest, materially limited sensitivity to generation‑level contamination: when no high‑confidence flags occurred, a single shared generation per item served both baseline and guarded conditions. We therefore treat the run as a methodological audit of preregistered controls under this sampling and generation regime and explicitly avoid generalizing results to web‑sourced public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and repair. Prior system and benchmark studies demonstrate that LLMs can synthesize network configurations and propose repairs under constrained settings; integrating external verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops typically improves average repair quality (e.g., recent agentic configuration repair and automatic repair systems). Formal verification tools and localized subspecification methods (Header Space Analysis, NetKAT‑family approaches) are practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are widely used in produce–validate pipelines.

Evaluation validity and contamination. Meta‑analyses and surveys identify contamination (benchmark content present in training corpora) and templating (low‑complexity items) as persistent threats to external validity for LLM evaluation. They recommend contamination detection (exact + fuzzy matching, provenance tracing), conservative guarded exclusions, and recording detector outputs at granular levels to support posterior adjudication. Our audit implements a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered confirmatory design and focuses on the operational effect of applying guarded exclusions on validator outcomes, rather than enumerating contamination prevalence in public benchmarks.

Positioning. Compared to broader benchmarking work that reports absolute capability, this study isolates the methodological impact of a preregistered contamination control pipeline under deterministic synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics. The nearest works motivate the need for auditor designs that (a) sample provenance‑rich items, (b) generate independent condition outputs, and (c) record granular detector scores; our reconciliation shows how failing to satisfy (a)–(c) collapses the paired test.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration summary. We preregistered the confirmatory design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs, tested with exact McNemar two‑sided test and accompanied by a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified detectors, thresholds, sampling rules, exclusion/replacement logic, analysis executors, and missingness handling.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). Detectors: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to the model public cutoff. Guarded policy: deterministically exclude high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replace them using deterministic retemplating and topology augmentation from the same generator with fixed seeds. Replacements must satisfy an embedding‑similarity constraint (preregistered) and pass functional checks before inclusion. These procedures and transformation semantics are archived in the transformation manifest.

Sampling, generation semantics, and verifiers (executed). The preregistration allowed deterministic task generation for reproducibility. The execution used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic intent→configuration tasks (source_identifier: "synthetic-netops:") for the 150‑item confirmatory sample. The run set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): when no exclusions occur, a single shared model generation per item is reused for baseline and guarded episodes. The verification oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5: a parse→state→property checker that returns a binary pass/fail under full_intent_constraint_validation and emits rich validator traces (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state, violation codes). Per‑episode scoring and validator traces were archived for reproducibility.

Planned analyses and sensitivities. The prespecified primary test used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with McNemar and paired bootstrap CI. Prespecified sensitivity checks included treating failed calls as failures, fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity (0.50, 0.65, 0.80), and stratified subgroup analysis by templated vs realistic items. The preregistration included a power/precision discussion: the originally multi‑model plan had greater sensitivity to detect ~5 percentage‑point paired differences; the single‑model, shared‑generation execution has reduced sensitivity and larger minimal detectable effects.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution completed the preregistered planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the run used one shared generation per item and model_calls_used = 150 rather than two calls per pair; provider call accounting and deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm these counts.

Contamination detector outcomes. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample. The contamination_summary artifact contains no flagged episodes. The archived detector workflow recorded explicit fuzzy overlap outputs only for episodes meeting flagging criteria or requiring replacement handling; since no episodes met the high‑confidence threshold, no per‑item overlap score aggregates were written to the detector outputs. Therefore, and artifact‑groundedly, we cannot report min/median/percentile overlap statistics for this execution because the archived detector logs do not include those summaries when no flags were produced.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode responses and validator traces are archived and referenced in the execution bundle.

Representative exemplar. A representative archived episode (task‑000001 / pair‑000001) shows identical normalized_response and normalized_reference_answer: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up". The validator returned score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION) with parsed_command_count = 4 and final_state matching the intent. This exemplar and its raw response/trace are present in the archived responses and scoring directories and serve as a concrete illustration of the artifact structure.

Why the results are degenerate (artifact‑grounded explanation). Two execution facts mechanistically produced the degenerate null. First, the sampled items were synthetic and provenance‑stable (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5), so canonical exact matches to public corpus fingerprints and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps (≥0.80) did not occur. Second, independent_condition_generation = false caused a single shared model generation per item to be used for both baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions were triggered. Both facts are recorded in the archived model configuration and task manifest and together led to identical baseline and guarded outputs per item, making the paired comparison insensitive to generation‑level contamination effects in this run.
sections.discussion:
What this execution answers and limitations of inference. The artifact record answers the preregistered methodological question for this specific sampling and generation regime: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and the preregistered conservative detectors, do high‑confidence flags arise and do guarded exclusions alter validator pass rates? In this run the answer is no. This does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks, does not evaluate paraphrase‑level leakage, and does not generalize across models or multi‑seed generation semantics.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations. The preregistration→execution reconciliation yields concrete, artifact‑grounded audit improvements: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items to exercise detectors against web‑sourced leakage; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions use independent model generations and cannot collapse to a shared output; (3) include multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance; (4) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of flag status so auditors can report overlap distributions; and (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from execution artifacts showing synthetic provenance and shared generation semantics and from the empty contamination_summary artifact.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, verifier‑backed validators remain valuable oracles for functional correctness checks, but auditor designs must ensure sampling and generation semantics exercise detector capabilities. An audit intended to assess public benchmark leakage should avoid synthetic provenance and shared generation semantics. Implementing the recommendations will materially increase an audit's sensitivity to contamination and improve the evidentiary value of observed discordance between baseline and guarded conditions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We provide a preregistration→execution reconciliation, confirm deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector logging, and paraphrase‑sensitive detectors to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived in the execution bundle and are available for verification as recorded in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
